usage_notes.narrative: Cma9 appears as the tonic resolution target in the major-sounds progression. Ch.2 p.15: 'The fifth chord is G13b5 (or Db7+9b5) which resolves into Cma9.' The major-ninth voicing is the landing point, not a passing color.

G7 anchors the seventh-sounds section. Ch.2 p.15: 'The first three chords illustrate movement around G7. The next four chords illustrate a substitute turn-around back to G13, followed by a cycle seventh movement.' Dominant sevenths drive both the local turnaround and the extended cycle.

Pass specifies that chord-symbol qualifier order equals voice order bottom-to-top. Ch.2 p.20: 'These chord symbols are written so that the order of appearance of notes coincides with the spelling of the chord symbol. For example, D7+9+5 means D7 with the raised 9th next, and the raised 5th on top.' The altered dominant D7+9+5 exemplifies the convention.

Pass instructs sustaining the lead note from one dominant voicing to the next. Ch.2 p.24: 'NOTE: Try to sustain lead notes from one chord to the next. For example, C9 to F13, sustain the G on top.' The common G is held across the II–V motion rather than re-attacked.

The tritone substitute Db7+9b5 is presented as interchangeable with G13b5. Ch.2 p.15: 'The fifth chord is G13b5 (or Db7+9b5) which resolves into Cma9.' The parenthetical equivalence signals the substitution as a practical re-spelling, not a separate color.

The altered dominant D7+9+5 demonstrates the voicing-layer convention. Ch.2 p.20: 'D7+9+5 means D7 with the raised 9th next, and the raised 5th on top.' Each suffix maps directly to a voice layer ascending from the seventh-chord shell.

Pass treats diminished chords as freely interchangeable approach chords that can resolve to multiple targets. Ch.2 p.15: 'Resolve the last chord in this sequence into any chord. For example: (1) Dm7 — G7 — Cma7, or (2) Em7 — Eb9 — Dm9 — Db9.' The open-resolution prescription underscores diminished's non-committed approach function.

Pass explicitly substitutes diminished chords for 7b9 harmony in a minor-key context. Ch.2 p.15: 'Use of diminished chords for seventh flat ninth chord movement, utilizing the basic pattern of A7 — Dm — G7 — C.' The diminished voicing replaces the A7b9 functional slot while retaining the approach-tone content.

Augmented chords are held as a sustained color before resolving chromatically into a cycle. Ch.2 p.15: 'The first six chords are basically G aug. Movement is used chromatically to get to the basic cycle (A7 — D7 — G).' The prescription is to sustain the augmented sound across multiple voicings rather than move through it quickly.

G aug serves as the final resolution target in the half-diminished-to-augmented passage. Ch.2 p.15: 'A7b9 to Dm7b5 resolving finally to G aug.' The augmented chord receives the cadence rather than a tonic major, functioning as an open, unresolved color endpoint.

Dm7 initiates the minor-seventh-to-seventh passage and resolves via a chromatic intermediate. Ch.2 p.15: 'First four chords illustrate movement in Dm7, resolving into Ab13 to G13.' The chromatic Ab13 is inserted as an approach dominant between the ii-chord and the diatonic V13.

Dm7b5 appears as the ii° chord in a iiø–V7b9 minor cadence and again in a iiø–V aug context. Ch.2 p.15: 'A7b9 to Dm7b5 resolving finally to G aug' and 'Dm7b5 chords to G aug. Notice the chords used to obtain these sounds.' The half-diminished functions as the ii chord in both cadential sequences.

A7b9 precedes Dm7b5 in the iiø–V7b9 passage. Ch.2 p.15: 'A7b9 to Dm7b5 resolving finally to G aug.' The b9 dominant is the V chord in a minor-key iiø–V pairing, with the cadence landing on an augmented rather than a tonic minor chord.
